articles.heading: Purpose and Guiding Principles
articles.content:
These regulations deal with the investigation of suspected cheating incidents and other fair play violations. They supplement and clarify the provisions of the FIDE Charter, the FIDE Ethics and Disciplinary Code, and the Procedural Rules of the Fair Play Commission.

The FIDE Laws of Chess have introduced provisions against cheating:
- Article 12.2.1: The arbiter shall ensure fair play.
- Article 12.2.7: The arbiter shall follow the Anti-Cheating Rules or Guidelines.

It is therefore the arbiter's duty to prevent cheating by the players. The Laws also explicitly forbid electronic devices (Articles 11.3.1, 11.3.2, 11.3.3).

articles.heading: Definition of Cheating
articles.content:
"Cheating" means:
a) The deliberate use of electronic devices (Art. 11.3.2 FIDE Laws of Chess) or other sources of information or advice (Art. 11.3.1) during a game; or
b) The manipulation of chess competitions, including but not limited to: result manipulation, sandbagging, match-fixing, rating fraud, false identity, and deliberate participation in fictitious tournaments or games.

Sandbagging refers to deliberately playing below one's actual ability in order to lower one's rating to play in a future event with a higher handicap and consequently with a better chance of winning.

For the purposes of this regulation, attempts at cheating will be considered cheating.

articles.heading: Assumed Cheating and Z-Score Thresholds
articles.content:
There shall be a presumption of cheating if statistical analysis by a FIDE-validated and approved algorithm shows a Z-score above the official threshold.

Currently, only Prof. Kenneth W. Regan's methodology is approved by FIDE. His model uses three separate statistical tests: Move-Matching (MM), Equal-top value moves (EV) and Average Scaled Difference (ASD), combined into a single overall Z-score.

Thresholds:
a) For online chess: a threshold of 4.25 (natural frequency of one in almost 100,000)
b) For over-the-board chess: a threshold of 5.00 (natural frequency of one in almost 3.5 million)

These provisions apply if there is no other evidence. If other evidence is available, a Z-score of 2.50 or higher may be used in support.

articles.heading: Other Fair Play Violations
articles.content:
Other fair play violations include:
a) Over-the-board rule violation: OTB rule violations include bringing a phone into the playing hall, bringing other forbidden gadgets (e.g. wallets, smart glasses, pens, watches), being uncooperative with the Fair Play Team or Arbiter, refusing to be searched or scanned. The list of OTB rule violations is not exhaustive.

b) Online technical rule violation: Technical violations connected with the video conference system — disconnections, playing without a camera on, playing without a shared screen, playing without a microphone on — per se do not lead to the assumption that a cheating offence has been committed, however, the player can be penalised accordingly.

articles.heading: Jurisdiction of the Fair Play Commission
articles.content:
The Fair Play Commission (FPL) has jurisdiction in all cheating-related matters, including false accusations. People subject to FPL jurisdiction include any person with FIDE ID: players, supporting persons, and team captains.

All FIDE-rated over-the-board games are subject to FPL jurisdiction.

Cheating incidents occurring in tournaments requiring maximum and increased levels of protection must be reported to FPL. Cheating incidents in standard-level tournaments are to be referred to National Federations (NFs), except when they affect the awarding of FM/WFM titles, or involve a person holding FM/WFM, IM/WIM or GM/WGM title — such cases must be reported to FPL.

articles.heading: Complaints and Investigations
articles.content:
Investigations can be initiated based on:
a) An In-Tournament Complaint (ITC)
b) A Post-Tournament Complaint (PTC)
c) A report of the Chief Fair Play Officer or Chief Arbiter
d) FPL initiative
e) A request by the Ethics and Disciplinary Commission (EDC)

Any person with a FIDE Identity Number can file a complaint. All complaints must be submitted in writing to fpl@fide.com. Oral or informal complaints are not accepted. All complaints based solely on the assumption that a person is playing stronger than expected due to rating will be considered manifestly unfounded.

All information about complaints and investigations shall remain confidential until an investigation is completed.

articles.heading: Investigation Procedure
articles.content:
When a cheating incident is brought to the attention of FPL, an Investigatory Panel (IP) of up to three FPL members can be nominated. The IP considers physical, observational, and statistical evidence, and may gather additional evidence including GM opinion.

Players, organisers, arbiters, national federations, and other parties are all required to cooperate with the IP. Failure to do so may result in referral to EDC.

If the IP comes to the unanimous conclusion that no cheating occurred or there is not enough evidence to meet the standard of proof, it shall dismiss the complaint. Otherwise, FPL decides by majority vote whether to forward the case to EDC.

The statute of limitation is five years; in online events, one year after the last round.

articles.heading: Levels of Fair Play Protection
articles.content:
Events are classified into three levels of protection:

a) Maximum Protection (Level 1): All FIDE World Events; all major Continental Events; round-robins with average rating 2650+; events with prize funds exceeding EUR 100,000; FIDE Circuit and Zonal Tournaments at Level 1.

b) Increased Protection (Level 2): Minor Continental events; National Championships; Norm events (for GM/IM titles); events with prize funds EUR 15,000+; round-robins with average rating 2500+.

c) Standard Protection (Level 3): National Junior/Youth Championships; all remaining FIDE-rated competitions.

For Level 1 events, a Fair Play Team led by a Chief Fair Play Officer (CFPO) is appointed, with a ratio of 1 Fair Play Specialist per 50 players in GSC events.

articles.heading: Practical Guidance for Arbiters on Anti-Cheating
articles.content:
According to Article 11.3.3 of the FIDE Laws of Chess, the arbiter may require the player to allow his/her clothes, bags, or other items to be inspected, in private. The arbiter or authorised person shall be of the same gender as the player. Note: such searches are illegal in some countries.

An arbiter should know how to recognise suspicious behaviours:
- Visits only the same toilet cubicle repeatedly
- Frequent absences from the board, with subsequent moves matching computer recommendations
- Accepting information from spectators or team members

Arbiters are encouraged to use the FIDE Screening Tool with PGN games during a tournament. Finding that a player or spectator is using a chess program in the playing area calls for immediate action in conjunction with the Chief Arbiter.

The player making a complaint should be told not to tell anyone else of their suspicions, as that could contaminate evidence.

articles.heading: Chief Arbiter – Chief Fair Play Officer Division of Tasks
articles.content:
The Chief Arbiter (CA) and the Chief Fair Play Officer (CFPO) have distinct but complementary responsibilities:

The Chief Arbiter is responsible for applying the Laws of Chess, administering the competition, and handling game-related incidents.

The Chief Fair Play Officer is responsible for devising and implementing the fair play plan, coordinating the Fair Play Team, conducting random and post-game checks, sending games for screening, and preparing the final fair play report.

At Level 1 events, the CFPO shall be invited to Organizing Team meetings as early as practicable. The CFPO and CA must coordinate closely. At events where no CFPO is appointed, In-Tournament Complaints should be addressed to the Chief Arbiter.

A list of prohibited items in the playing area must be jointly identified by the CA and CFPO and listed in the tournament regulations.
